dossier.public_summary: The dip sits on the target star but the star shows strong astrometric wobble and a huge out-of-eclipse wiggle equal to the dip depth, with the dip depth changing by a factor of ~6 between sectors. Together this matches a close stellar companion (ellipsoidal eclipsing binary) that mimics a short-period transit, not a 5.6 Earth-radius planet.

reasons.why: RUWE 7.5 is far above the astrometric single-star threshold and signals the target is an astrometric binary / double system
Extreme Gaia excess noise and ipd_multi_peak 1 corroborate the star is not a single star
Variability at the transit period is as large as the dip itself, which is not explained by a planet and is typical of ellipsoidal / reflection from a close, tidally distorted stellar companion

Depth changes dramatically between sectors (e.g., sector 2 9381 ppm vs sector 30 1585 ppm) in a way expected for ellipsoidal modulation from a binary filling its Roche lobe as ellipsoidal amplitude varies with geometry/phases, not a stable planet
Difference imaging puts the dip on the target (suspects ruled out at 77+ sigma), so the ellipsoidal signal is on-target and not a neighbour blend
Low planet score as one of ten, consistent with checks favouring a binary over a planet
